\section*{S1. The Rating Platform}

This section describes the platform (version \texttt{v1.0-heights-film}) in more detail than the main text. Code
references are to the archived release; the platform documentation gives the full event definitions. Figure~\ref{fig:workflow} shows the session workflow.

\paragraph{Recording ratings.} A small affect grid is overlaid on the lower right of the video
(Figure~\ref{fig:task}). The mouse pointer is hidden and locked, so moving the mouse moves the dot without clicking;
arrow keys provide an alternative. Horizontal position codes valence (0~=~unpleasant, 100~=~pleasant) and vertical
position arousal (0~=~low, 100~=~high). The position is sampled at 20~Hz, and each sample stores the video time, the
media time of the last frame presented (where the browser reports it), the elapsed time since the film started and
whether the film was playing. Every input event is also stored unsmoothed, so that the rating series can be
reconstructed from the raw input.

\paragraph{Controlling presentation.} The whole film is downloaded before playback starts, and sessions that cannot
download it within 5~min end early. Player controls are hidden and seeking is blocked. Hiding the tab, leaving full
screen or losing the pointer lock pauses the film behind a \enquote{Continue} screen, and the number and duration of
such interruptions, as well as any buffering, are logged. Data are sent to the server every 30~s of film; after a page
reload, the session resumes shortly before the last saved point.

\paragraph{Training.} Before the film, participants practise with the same pointer-locked mouse control in two steps.
First, for 40~s they keep the dot on an orange target that moves around the grid without the film: it rests for 6~s in
each corner and 4~s at the centre, then glides diagonally to a final point, so that every combination of valence and
arousal is visited. Accuracy is the mean distance between dot and target (0--100 units), ignoring the first 1.5~s after
each jump of the target; if it exceeds 20 units, the practice is repeated once.

Second, a page explains the grid: left to right is unpleasant to pleasant, with neutral in the centre; down to up is
low to high activation, where activation means \enquote{feeling activated or stirred up, regardless of whether the
feeling is pleasant or unpleasant}. It adds that the same area can hold quite different feelings: being nervous and
being angry are both unpleasant with high activation (upper left), while being sad or bored is unpleasant with low
activation (lower left). Participants then read six situations in random order. For each, they move the dot to where
that feeling belongs and press the space bar; the expected quadrant is then highlighted and a one-sentence explanation
is shown. A placement counts as correct if it lies in the expected quadrant at least 5 units from both midlines. The
six situations, with the expected quadrant and the explanation shown, were:
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
\item \enquote{You are waiting for important test results and your heart is pounding.} Unpleasant, high activation:
  \enquote{Feeling nervous or tense is unpleasant, with high activation.}
\item \enquote{Someone pushes in front of you in a long queue and you feel your face getting hot.} Unpleasant, high
  activation: \enquote{Anger is also unpleasant with high activation -- this area holds many different feelings, not
  just fear.}
\item \enquote{After a long, disappointing day you feel tired and low.} Unpleasant, low activation: \enquote{Feeling
  sad or drained is unpleasant, with low activation.}
\item \enquote{You are stuck at home on a grey afternoon with nothing to do, feeling bored and sluggish.} Unpleasant,
  low activation: \enquote{Boredom is unpleasant, with low activation.}
\item \enquote{Your favourite team scores the winning goal in the last minute.} Pleasant, high activation:
  \enquote{Excitement is pleasant, with high activation.}
\item \enquote{You are lying in a warm bath after a good day.} Pleasant, low activation: \enquote{Relaxed contentment
  is pleasant, with low activation.}
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Assessing session quality.} Two instructed-response attention checks are given, one before and one after
the film. In text fields, pasting, dropping and copying text are blocked, and keystrokes and input types are logged.
Browser events not generated by a person (script-generated input) are counted. Quality-control code computes measures
of rating coverage, interruptions, buffering and rating activity, and flags a session for review if any of the
following occurs:
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
\item Viewing: more than 3 interruptions or more than 60~s interrupted; more than 30~s of buffering; more than 120~s
  away from the window; more than 180~s of film without any rating input.
\item Training: tracking error above 20 units after the last run; fewer than 3 of the 6 situations placed correctly.
\item Mouse movement: 3 or more isolated large jumps (a single movement of more than 250 pixels with no other mouse
  event within 100~ms on either side); more than 10\% of movements larger than 250 pixels; 30 or more identical
  consecutive movements of at least 3 pixels; 98\% or more of movements along one axis only (with at least 200
  movements).
\item Text entry: fewer than 0.2 keystrokes per character (texts of at least 200 characters); typing faster than 700
  characters per minute; two or more different phrasing markers (below); 80\% or more similarity to another
  participant's text (sequence-matching ratio).
\end{itemize}
The phrasing markers are words and characters that are common in text produced by large language models and rare in
quick participant writing: \textit{delve}, \textit{tapestry}, \textit{navigate/navigating the}, \textit{testament
to}, \textit{in conclusion}, \textit{overall,}, \textit{it's worth noting}, \textit{as an AI}, \textit{language model},
\textit{visceral}, \textit{palpable}, \textit{juxtapose} (and related forms), \textit{underscore(s/d)}, \textit{a
sense of awe/unease/vertigo}, \textit{heightened sense}, \textit{multifaceted} and the em dash. A match is a reason to
read the text, not evidence of assistance: several markers are words an attentive viewer of this film could use.
Flags only prompted review; participants were excluded solely by the registered rules (Table~\ref{tab:screening}), which overlap with
some of these criteria. The written account served as evidence about participation; analysis of its content is outside
the scope of this report.

\section*{S3. Confirmatory Tests and Sensitivity Analyses}

Table~\ref{tab:confirmatory} lists all preregistered tests in the primary sample, and Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}
repeats them in the two preregistered sensitivity samples. The stricter-engagement sample
($n$~=~\val{n_stricter}) additionally excluded sparse raters (fewer than one rating bout per minute, or more than 180~s
without input; \val{n_sparse}), participants who failed one attention check (\val{n_one_check}) and participants who
reported not watching attentively (\val{n_not_attentive}); these groups overlap. The second sample
($n$~=~\val{n_without_rejected}) excluded the \val{n_rejection_set} participants whose Prolific submissions were
rejected for behaviour on the free-text page but who passed the registered exclusion rules. Figure~\ref{fig:segments}
shows segment means and Figure~\ref{fig:correlations} the individual-difference tests.

\section*{S4. Registered Descriptive Analyses}

Split-half reliability of the group-mean series (1,000 random splits, Spearman--Brown corrected) was \val{rel:arousal}
for arousal and \val{rel:valence} for valence. Re-estimating the segment edges in the confirmatory sample with the
registered piecewise-linear method (three breakpoints, minimum segment length 30~s; 1,000 participant bootstrap
resamples) gave \val{edge1:est}~s \val{edge1:ci}, \val{edge2:est}~s \val{edge2:ci} and \val{edge3:est}~s
\val{edge3:ci}, against the registered \val{edge1:reg}, \val{edge2:reg} and \val{edge3:reg}~s. All tests used the fixed
registered edges.

\section*{S5. Exploratory Analyses}

In a post hoc exploratory analysis, the change in each STICSA somatic item was examined: for each item, the mean change, the share of participants whose answer increased and $d_z$, with Wilcoxon
signed-rank tests Holm-corrected across the 11 items (Table~\ref{tab:items}).

\input{generated/table_items.tex}

The registration anticipated exploratory affect-grid and age/sex analyses without specifying confirmatory tests.
Figure~\ref{fig:grid} shows where on the affect grid participants spent their time in each segment. For age and sex
(Prolific profile data; $n$~=~\val{n_demo}
with both available), the STICSA change was regressed on sex and age, and segment means were modelled with a
random-intercept mixed model including segment (sum-coded) $\times$ (sex + age), with likelihood-ratio tests of the
interactions; the same model fitted by least squares with participant-clustered standard errors is reported as a check
(Table~\ref{tab:agesex}, Figures~\ref{fig:sexcourse} and \ref{fig:agesex}). The age/sex models were specified before
running them on the confirmatory sample; their $p$ values are uncorrected.

\section*{S6. Notes on the Preregistered Plan}

H6 was added when preparing the registration, after inspection of a descriptive group-mean plot and before any
confirmatory hypothesis test. H1--H5 and their analysis plan were unchanged.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The registration reported 123 usable confirmatory participants at submission; one further participant completed
the study after that count, had complete data and passed all exclusion rules, and was included as registered
($N$~=~\val{n_primary}).
\item The fixed segment edges were estimated on 22 exploratory participants under the quality-control rules in use at
the time; under the final registered rules 21 are usable, and these form the reference curve for H3.
\item \enquote{Reported not watching attentively} was implemented as answering \enquote{No}; participants who answered
\enquote{Mostly} were retained.
\item Before the confirmatory run, the segment-edge bootstrap was set to 1,000 participant resamples; the
registration did not specify a number. Bootstraps used seed 20261004, and Spearman confidence intervals were
percentile intervals. H1 was treated as a single-test family, with the Wilcoxon check reported alongside; H3 was
decided by its confidence-interval criterion without a $p$ value.
\item Exploratory age and sex analyses used segment-level mixed models; models over the 1-Hz series, mentioned in
the registration as an example, were not implemented. Alternative optimisation algorithms were tried when needed
for convergence, without changing the model or decision rule.
\end{enumerate}
